To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the hydraulic conductance of leaf laminae (Klamina), which substantially constrains wholeplant water transport, was co-ordinated among temperate woody plants with traits associated with maximum rates of water and gas exchange, but was independent of traits associated with carbon economy, drought tolerance, and other traits.

the hydraulic conductance of sun leaves is 15–67 per cent higher than that of shade leaves, and that the hydraulic conductances of leaves of different species are co-ordinated with leaf structural traits that are associated with high rates of water and gas transport, but are independent of leaf structural traits that may be associated with drought tolerance or carbon economy.

the hydraulic conductance of leaf laminae (Klamina, kg m−2 s −1 MPa −1), which substantially constrains whole‐plant water transport, is correlated with traits relating to maximum rates of water transport and gas exchange in the lamina, but is independent of other traits that are associated with drought tolerance or with carbon economy.

the co-ordination of leaf traits relating to water transport and gas exchange.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Klamina of sun leaves is co-ordinated with the hydraulic conductance of leaves as a whole and with traits associated with the liquid-phase transport of water in leaves, and that it is independent of other leaf traits.

Klamina of the lamina of leaves of temperate woody plants is co-ordinated with the hydraulic conductance of their petioles, and with the structure and functioning of their stomata, and is independent of other leaf traits.

the ‘hydrology’ (i.e. liquid-phase water transport) of leaves is co-ordinated with other aspects of the leaf hydrologic system, but independent of traits relating to drought avoidance or carbon economy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for temperate woody plants, leaf lamina hydraulic conductance is a function of leaf irradiance, leaf water storage capacitance and mesophyll resistance, and is independent of leaf carbon economy and drought tolerance traits.

, in the six species studied, Klamina is co-ordinated with a subset of leaf traits that relate to the hydraulic conductance of lamina tissues and to the capacity for high rates of water and CO2 flux, but is not co-ordinated with other traits that may be associated with leaf drought tolerance.
leaf hydraulic conductance is co-ordinated with leaf structure and physiology, in a way that is consistent with the hypothesis that Klamina is a major determinant of whole-plant water use.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Klamina is a trait of considerable importance for the functioning of woody leaves in temperate environments.

Klamina is co‐ordinated with leaf traits associated with high rates of gas exchange and liquid‐phase water transport, and that this co‐ordination is independent of leaf traits associated with drought tolerance and aspects of carbon economy.
Klamina is a key trait for understanding leaf water transport.
